newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In - sound bites back on World Wide Web.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In - sound bites back on World Wide Web.

text.p: Maybe we should just stick our heads in the sand regarding "pirated" intellectual property on the World Wide Web.
Or we could take the advice of Noel Gallagher, guitarist for the British group Oasis.

"I don't own a computer. I don't wish to own a computer. I have absolutely no interest in what is going on between Sony music and the Web sites," Gallagher recently told MTV Latino. "Computers are rubbish, buy guitars, that's all I'm saying."
Well, many Oasis fans have computers and have been posting sites on the Internet's World Wide Web in dedication.

While Gallagher may not mind, some of the pages have been liberally borrowing music clips and other material owned by the band and its record company. Gallagher could do well to check out the sites and even stop by his own band's official site: http://www.oasisinet.com.
The Financial Times reported last month that Oasis issued warnings to many of the Web sites in a bid to clamp down against copyright infringements on the Net.

"In its warning to unauthorized Oasis web sites, Ignition Management says it is unlawful to use copyrighted photographs, video clips and sound samples without permission, and has given them 30 days to erase illegal material," the Financial Times reported.

But Ignition Management, which manages Oasis, probably is not interested in going after every last Web site. It is more worried about groups or individuals who profit by building commercial Web sites or bootleggers who need material for counterfeit recordings.
Joining the fray earlier this month was the Recording Industry Association of America, which has launched its own assault on illegal use of sound recordings on the Net.
Variety reported that federal judges in Texas and New York have shut down Web sites in those states for posting digital recordings on the Web.

"As we embrace today's newest technology -- the Internet -- it's important to remember our values count, even in cyberspace," association President Hilary Rosen said, according to Variety, the entertainment industry publication.

The Clinton administration and other governments are grappling with how to enforce copyright issues in the digital age. Many in cyberspace believe "old world" laws have no bearing on the new digital world and fiercely oppose what they see as attempts at censorship on the Net.

A good case in point is "The Official Oasis Webmasters for Internet Freedom Homepage," (http://falcon.cc.ukans.edu/jackm/OWIF.htm) which was set up by Jack Martin, a University of Kansas student who also operates his own Oasis site.

The site contains a list of Oasis sites that have been recently closed, a word by Noel Gallagher claiming the band did not know about the crackdown and the letter from band management on the "fair use" issue.

Martin, of course, is objecting to the heavy handedness against Web sites that provide free advertising for groups like Oasis. And there is the larger concern that once the censorship dogs are let loose on the Internet the place just won't be the same.
Many on the Web probably support efforts such as Martin's. But the intellectual property issue is not only backed by artists but also by corporate interests and legal talent.

Perhaps it would be fitting to close with the words from the Oasis song "Listen Up" (as supplied by Martin): "Day by day, there's a man in a suit who's gonna make you pay/For the thoughts that you think and the words they won't let you say."
